"Billboard Hot 100") on the issue dated December 14, 2019,[\[80\]](#cite_note-cbc082021-81) but fell 41 places to number 52 in its second week.[\[81\]](#cite_note-82) In its 12th week on the chart, the song became the Weeknd's tenth top ten hit by rising to a new peak at number ten.[\[82\]](#cite_note-83) On the issue dated March 28, 2020, the song rose two places to reach number two.[\[83\]](#cite_note-84) The song reached number one on [R&B/Hip-Hop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R&B/Hip-Hop_Songs "R&B/Hip-Hop Songs") on April 4, 2020, leading for 11 non-consecutive weeks.[\[84\]](#cite_note-Trust-85) The song also reached number one on [R&B Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/R&B_Songs "R&B Songs") chart on March 7, 2020, where it became his seventh number one on the chart, making him the artist with the most number ones on the chart's history and also attaining a record-breaking reign of 48 weeks.[\[85\]](#cite_note-86) On March 30, 2020, the song rose to number one on the _Billboard_ Hot 100, dethroning [Roddy Ricch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roddy_Ricch "Roddy Ricch")'s "[The Box](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Box_\(Roddy_Ricch_song\) "The Box (Roddy Ricch song)")" on the issue dated April 4, 2020.[\[86\]](#cite_note-BH100_Peak-87) The single kept at its peak position the following week, becoming the Weeknd's third multi-week leader after "[The Hills](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hills_\(song\) "The Hills (song)")", which topped the chart five years earlier.[\[87\]](#cite_note-88) "Blinding Lights" spent four weeks atop the Hot 100 and finished 2020 as the [year's top _Billboard_ Hot 100 song](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Year-End_Hot_100_singles_of_2020 "Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 2020").[\[88\]](#cite_note-BBNo1OfYear-89) The following year, it ranked at number three on the year-end chart, becoming the first single to finish in the top three on two occasions.[\[89\]](#cite_note-90)

"Blinding Lights" spent 57 weeks in the top ten of the _Billboard_ Hot 100 and 43 weeks in the top five, breaking the record for the most time logged in the region over the chart's 62-year history.[\[90\]](#cite_note-billboard.com-91)[\[91\]](#cite_note-BillboardUSCert-92) On the [Digital Song Sales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_Songs "Digital Songs") chart, the song peaked at number one for the week of March 23, 2020, and became the Weeknd's fifth Digital Songs number one. The single reached a peak of number one on the [Streaming Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Streaming_Songs "Streaming Songs") chart on March 30, becoming his first topper on the listing since "The Hills" led five years earlier.[\[92\]](#cite_note-93) On April 13, the song reached number one on [Pop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_Songs "Pop Songs") chart, where it led for 6 non-consecutive weeks, as it slid to number two on the Hot 100.[\[93\]](#cite_note-94) It later rose back up to number one for the two following weeks.[\[94\]](#cite_note-95)[\[95\]](#cite_note-BB4thweek-96)[\[96\]](#cite_note-97) On May 18, the song became his first number one on the [Adult Pop Songs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adult_Pop_Songs "Adult Pop Songs") chart, leading for 20 non-consecutive weeks.[\[97\]](#cite_note-98) On November 7, "Blinding Lights" became his first

# Blinding Lights

ax Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), saying: "Max and I have become literally the best of friends, but I don't do that with many people. It's not that I can't, but a collaboration is a relationship, it's like a marriage, you've gotta build up to it."[\[15\]](#cite_note-15) In a _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ interview, the Weeknd expressed his appreciation for [music of the 1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_music "1980s in music"): "I've always had an admiration for the era before I was born. You can hear it as far back as my [first mixtape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Balloons "House of Balloons") that the '80s — [Siouxsie and the Banshees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siouxsie_and_the_Banshees "Siouxsie and the Banshees"), [Cocteau Twins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cocteau_Twins "Cocteau Twins") — play such a huge role in my sound. Sometimes it helps me create a new sound and sometimes it's just obvious. I'm just glad the world's into it now."[\[16\]](#cite_note-16) In an interview with _[Vanity Fair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanity_Fair_\(magazine\) "Vanity Fair (magazine)")_, the Weeknd said that he initially thought that the song would be a commercial failure.[\[17\]](#cite_note-17)

## Lyrics and composition

\[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Blinding_Lights&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Lyrics and composition")\]

Throughout the song, the Weeknd sings about the rekindling of a relationship and the importance of his partner. He also mentions the city of [Las Vegas, Nevada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Las_Vegas,_Nevada "Las Vegas, Nevada"), when he refers to it by its nickname "Sin City" in the [pre-chorus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pre-chorus "Pre-chorus").[\[18\]](#cite_note-18) In a profile in [_Esquire_ magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Esquire_\(magazine\) "Esquire (magazine)"), The Weeknd explained that "'Blinding Lights' \[is about\] how you want to see someone at night, and you're intoxicated, and you're driving to this person and you're just blinded by streetlights, but nothing could stop you from trying to go see that person, because you're so lonely. I don't want to ever promote drunk driving, but that's what the dark undertone is."[\[19\]](#cite_note-19)

From its scale-laddering verses to its tension-filled chorus, the song exhibits the polish and "melodic math" for which [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin") is renowned, according to Chris Molanphy from _[Slate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slate_\(magazine\) "Slate (magazine)")_.[\[20\]](#cite_note-20) The [Dorian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorian_mode "Dorian mode") structure provides a dreamy and euphoric nature to the song while still ultimately resolving to a minor chord. Exclusively in the music video, the song temporarily modulates to E♭ Dorian as the [beats per minute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beats_per_minute "Beats per minute") drops for 3 and a half measures.

_[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ staff writer Frank DiGiacomo assessed its qualities, "The opening drumbeat is a [DeLorean \[time machine\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DeLorean_time_machine "DeLorean time machine") [back to](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Back_to_the_Future "Back to the Future") [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson")'s '[Beat It](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_It "Beat It")'. The [amphetamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amphetamine "Amphetamine") [synth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthesizer "Synthesizer") conjures fond memories of leopard-print-era [Rod Stewart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rod_Stewart "Rod Stewart")'s '[Young Turks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young_Turks_\(song\) "Young Turks (song)")' — or maybe that other guy with the avian hairdo, [Mike Score](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Score "Mike Score") from [A Flock of Seagulls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Flock_of_Seagulls "A Flock of Seagulls")? And isn't that spooky B-movie [organ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organ_\(music\) "Organ (music)") from [Rockwell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockwell_\(musician\) "Rockwell (musician)")'s '[Somebody's Watching Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somebody's_Watching_Me "Somebody's Watching Me")'? Abel Tesfaye's [Drambuie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drambuie "Drambuie")\-drenched vocals bathe you in euphoria as you bop around your home in an [N-95](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N95_mask "N95 mask") mask, punching your fist to the 'Hey!-Hey!-Hey!''s, making a magical and much-needed tonic for troubled times".[\[21\]](#cite_note-billboard2020-21)

The genre of the song is generally described as [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"), [synthwave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthwave "Synthwave") and [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop"). Audio engineer [Şerban Ghenea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serban_Ghenea "Serban Ghenea") says he loved working on the Weeknd's crisp-sounding "Blinding Lights". "It was crossing two worlds to make something new that fits today, sonically. The older folks like it because it's a throwback, and then the kids love it because it's a new thing that they never heard before."[\[22\]](#cite_note-22)

"Blinding Lights" received universal acclaim from critics.[\[23\]](#cite_note-23)[\[24\]](#cite_note-guardian-24)[\[25\]](#cite_note-nytimes-25)[\[26\]](#cite_note-billboard-26) It was named as the second best song of 2020 by _[Billboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_\(magazine\) "Billboard (magazine)")_ and the best song of 2020 by _[Consequence of Sound](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consequence_of_Sound "Consequence of Sound")_; the former highlighted its nostalgic appeal,[\[27\]](#cite_note-BB100Best2020-27) and the latter praised its "melodic romance waxed over a blockbuster riff".[\[28\]](#cite_note-28) _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")_ magazine named "Blinding Lights" the Record of the Year: "The Weeknd's 'Blinding Lights' is indisputably one of the landmark songs of 2020. The piece has a crystalline synth hook straight out of 1985. The record has come to symbolize strength and triumphing over adversity."[\[29\]](#cite_note-VarietyHitmaker-29) "Blinding Lights" was named one of the best songs of 2019 by _[Stereogum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stereogum "Stereogum")_, where editor Chris DeVille complimented the song's '80s aesthetic and vibe, saying that "the '80s will never die—or, at least, the glamorous neon '80s of our collective imagination".[\[30\]](#cite_note-30)

_[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ columnist Kory Grow named "Blinding Lights" as the fourth best song of 2020: "With fuzzy synths and hopscotching [drum-machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drum_machine "Drum machine") line, 'Blinding Lights' is the best [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music") song this side of [Duran Duran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duran_Duran "Duran Duran"). In just three minutes, the Weeknd checks off any number of Eighties pop-song signposts—unanswered phone calls, driving fast just to feel something, lights representing loneliness—but the real magic is how his voice and the song's chiming [keyboard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keyboard_instrument "Keyboard instrument") line lingers in your head well after he injects new life into the greatest Eighties-steeped lyrical cliché of them all: 'I can't sleep until I feel your touch,'" and editor Jon Dolan praised the "[europhile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europhile "Europhile") [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop")\-ste

_**Hurry Up Tomorrow**_ is the sixth studio album by the Canadian singer-songwriter [the Weeknd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weeknd "The Weeknd"). It was released through [XO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XO_\(record_label\) "XO (record label)") and [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records") on January 31, 2025. It also serves as a companion piece to [the film of the same name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurry_Up_Tomorrow_\(film\) "Hurry Up Tomorrow (film)"). The standard album contains guest appearances from [Anitta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anitta_\(singer\) "Anitta (singer)"), [Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_\(band\) "Justice (band)"), [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott"), [Florence and the Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_and_the_Machine "Florence and the Machine"), [Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_\(rapper\) "Future (rapper)"), [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti"), [Giorgio Moroder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Moroder "Giorgio Moroder"), and [Lana Del Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lana_Del_Rey "Lana Del Rey"), with a bonus edition containing an additional appearance from [Swedish House Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_House_Mafia "Swedish House Mafia").[\[4\]](#cite_note-Aswad-5) Production was primarily handled by the Weeknd himself and his regular collaborators including [Cirkut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirkut "Cirkut"), [DaHeala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DaHeala "DaHeala"), [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), [Mike Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dean_\(producer\) "Mike Dean (producer)"), [Metro Boomin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Boomin "Metro Boomin"), Prince85 and [OPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneohtrix_Point_Never "Oneohtrix Point Never"), alongside various other producers.

_Hurry Up Tomorrow_ is primarily a [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B") album, while exploring a wide variety of genres such as [Brazilian funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_funk "Brazilian funk") and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop").[\[5\]](#cite_note-6) The album is the final installment of a trilogy following the Weeknd's previous two studio albums, _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ (2020) and _[Dawn FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_FM "Dawn FM")_ (2022). The Weeknd has hinted _Hurry Up Tomorrow_ may be his final album under his stage name,[\[6\]](#cite_note-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-8) and revealed that it was partly inspired by losing his voice while on tour in 2022.[\[1\]](#cite_note-NME-1)[\[3\]](#cite_note-independent-3)[\[8\]](#cite_note-telegraph-9) _Hurry Up Tomorrow_ was supported by the singles "[Timeless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeless_\(The_Weeknd_and_Playboi_Carti_song\) "Timeless (The Weeknd and Playboi Carti song)")", "[São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo_\(song\) "São Paulo (song)")", and "[Cry for Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cry_for_Me_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Cry for Me (The Weeknd song)")". To promote the album, a co-headlining extension of [his tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_til_Dawn_Tour "After Hours til Dawn Tour") with [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti") kicked off in summer 2025 and is set to end in 2026.

_Hurry Up Tomorrow_ opened with first-week sales of 490,500 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_units "Album-equivalent units") in the U.S. and debuted at number one on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), marking the Weeknd's fifth number-one album on the chart. Internationally, it topped the charts in 16 countries, including in Canada, France, Norway, Belgium, Australia, the United Kingdom, and New Zealand. The album received positive reviews from critics, with praise for its production, lyrical content and vocal performances; some critics described _Hurry Up Tomorrow_ as a "powerful finale" to the trilogy and [alter ego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alter_ego "Alter ego") of the Weeknd.[\[9\]](#cite_note-BD-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

On March 25, 2020, the Weeknd previewed five unreleased tracks during an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") livestream,[\[11\]](#cite_note-US-12) some of which were reportedly intended for _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ (2020),[\[12\]](#cite_note-MT-13) which was released five days prior. Three songs—"Nothing Compares", "Missed You", and "Final Lullaby"—were later added as bonus tracks in the deluxe edition of the album.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14) However, the other tracks, "Take Me Back to LA" and "The Abyss" (then listed as "Regular" or "Hold My Heart"), did not appear

The standard album contains guest appearances from [Anitta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anitta_\(singer\) "Anitta (singer)"), [Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justice_\(band\) "Justice (band)"), [Travis Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travis_Scott "Travis Scott"), [Florence and the Machine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_and_the_Machine "Florence and the Machine"), [Future](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_\(rapper\) "Future (rapper)"), [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti"), [Giorgio Moroder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Moroder "Giorgio Moroder"), and [Lana Del Rey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lana_Del_Rey "Lana Del Rey"), with a bonus edition containing an additional appearance from [Swedish House Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_House_Mafia "Swedish House Mafia").[\[4\]](#cite_note-Aswad-5) Production was primarily handled by the Weeknd himself and his regular collaborators including [Cirkut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cirkut "Cirkut"), [DaHeala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DaHeala "DaHeala"), [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), [Mike Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dean_\(producer\) "Mike Dean (producer)"), [Metro Boomin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Boomin "Metro Boomin"), Prince85 and [OPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneohtrix_Point_Never "Oneohtrix Point Never"), alongside various other producers.

_Hurry Up Tomorrow_ is primarily a [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B") album, while exploring a wide variety of genres such as [Brazilian funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazilian_funk "Brazilian funk") and [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip-hop "Hip-hop").[\[5\]](#cite_note-6) The album is the final installment of a trilogy following the Weeknd's previous two studio albums, _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ (2020) and _[Dawn FM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_FM "Dawn FM")_ (2022). The Weeknd has hinted _Hurry Up Tomorrow_ may be his final album under his stage name,[\[6\]](#cite_note-7)[\[7\]](#cite_note-8) and revealed that it was partly inspired by losing his voice while on tour in 2022.[\[1\]](#cite_note-NME-1)[\[3\]](#cite_note-independent-3)[\[8\]](#cite_note-telegraph-9) _Hurry Up Tomorrow_ was supported by the singles "[Timeless](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeless_\(The_Weeknd_and_Playboi_Carti_song\) "Timeless (The Weeknd and Playboi Carti song)")", "[São Paulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/São_Paulo_\(song\) "São Paulo (song)")", and "[Cry for Me](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cry_for_Me_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Cry for Me (The Weeknd song)")". To promote the album, a co-headlining extension of [his tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_til_Dawn_Tour "After Hours til Dawn Tour") with [Playboi Carti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Playboi_Carti "Playboi Carti") kicked off in summer 2025 and is set to end in 2026.

_Hurry Up Tomorrow_ opened with first-week sales of 490,500 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_units "Album-equivalent units") in the U.S. and debuted at number one on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"), marking the Weeknd's fifth number-one album on the chart. Internationally, it topped the charts in 16 countries, including in Canada, France, Norway, Belgium, Australia, the United Kingdom, and New Zealand. The album received positive reviews from critics, with praise for its production, lyrical content and vocal performances; some critics described _Hurry Up Tomorrow_ as a "powerful finale" to the trilogy and [alter ego](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alter_ego "Alter ego") of the Weeknd.[\[9\]](#cite_note-BD-10)[\[10\]](#cite_note-11)

On March 25, 2020, the Weeknd previewed five unreleased tracks during an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") livestream,[\[11\]](#cite_note-US-12) some of which were reportedly intended for _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ (2020),[\[12\]](#cite_note-MT-13) which was released five days prior. Three songs—"Nothing Compares", "Missed You", and "Final Lullaby"—were later added as bonus tracks in the deluxe edition of the album.[\[13\]](#cite_note-14) However, the other tracks, "Take Me Back to LA" and "The Abyss" (then listed as "Regular" or "Hold My Heart"), did not appear

text:
# The Weeknd’s Endless Summer

[  
T  
he Weeknd](https://www.rollingstone.com/t/the-weeknd/) promises he hasn’t baked any bread during quarantine, unlike every other bored millennial on Instagram.

“I’m a horrible cook,” he says, laughing off the very idea, on a Zoom call from a desk in a tastefully decorated, exceptionally long room in his home on Los Angeles’ west side. A black bookshelf behind him displays monochromatic vases, while the wall-mounted TV in the background silently plays commercials. He’s lived in L.A. for about six years now, including a few years in a $20 million mansion in the gated community of Hidden Hills, where his neighbors included Drake, Britney Spears, and the Kardashians. He’s spent so much of the past decade touring the world, though, that he still sees his birthplace, Toronto, as his real home. “I didn’t realize how nice Canadians were until I left Canada,” he says.

The 30-year-old hitmaker, born Abel Tesfaye, is wearing a plain black shirt, and tomorrow he’ll reappear in a similarly understated white jersey. It’s a little jarring to see him in anything other than the slick red suit and bright-orange vintage-style frames he’s been sporting most of this year, as part of the action-packed, conceptual promotional campaign for his fourth album, _After Hours_.

As an asthmatic, Tesfaye has been taking extra precautions since the pandemic began. He works with a small group of people that includes photographer Nabil Elderkin and a few trusted affiliates and friends from his label, XO, all of whom get tested for Covid-19 every two weeks. In August, he celebrated the birthday of his Doberman, Caesar, with a cake for his “son” that he definitely didn’t bake himself. And he’s been watching movies — lots of movies, mostly ultraviolent Korean cinema. (_The Wailing,_ a 2016 horror film about a mysterious plague, and _I Saw the Devil,_ a 2010 action thriller about a man on a revenge mission, are two of his favorites.) He recently finished _Waco_ and _Unsolved Mysteries,_ among other Netflix and Hulu shows he’s been bingeing to pass the time. Sometimes he writes songs to the scenes and characters onscreen. “I’ll write about their relationship or something in a song,” he says. “It might never see the light of day. That’s an exercise. I love doing that.”

## Editor’s picks

There’s been a lot of time to fill lately, ever since he had to postpone or cancel months of touring and other promotional plans meant to follow the release of his album. “I’ve been going kind of mad, actually,” he admits.

Truthfully, though, sheltering in place hasn’t been all that different from how he usually works. Tesfaye, who has called himself a “workaholic,” put together _After Hours_ at studios in New York, Los Angeles, Toronto, and right here at home. It took two years, and he ended up building his most fully-realized world yet, an ambitious visual and musical cycle full of bruising fights, shady figures, dizzying neon lights, and inner demons. The druggy vibe and nihilistic lyrics of tracks like “Faith” and “Heartless” hearken back to a more turbulent time in his past, evoking his very public 2015 arrest for allegedly punching a Las Vegas cop, and assorted other benders.

To promote the album, he’s embraced a level of campiness he has only hinted at before, diving bloodied and bandaged nose-first into a spiraling, self-destructive character straight out of a David Lynch film. Every photo shoot, music video, and TV performance has been an extension of his fun-house-mirror world.

For Tesfaye, that immersive work scratched an itch that goes back to his earliest independent mixtapes, starting with 2011’s _House of Balloons._ The vision he brought to the photo shoots and music videos for those projects, which were compiled on 2012’s _Trilogy_ after he signed with Republic Records, created a mystique that was central to his appeal at the start of his career. “I’ve always tried to do what I do with _After Hours_ with every record I’ve ever done,” he says. “I just didn’t have the resources or the budget or the time to make them as cohesive and as singular as _After Hours_ was visually.”

The result is an album that puts him in contention for the 2021 Grammy Awards in several top categories, and one he’s immensely proud of. “It might not be my best album,” he says. “It might not be what people gravitate towards the most in the future. Hopefully it is. But to me, it’s definitely my most perfect album. I could go back and listen to it and be like, ‘I’ve got no notes for this, really.’ ”

## Related

![Lazy loaded image](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/GRAMMY_FEA_Weekend_B.jpg?w=768)

“I’ve been cooped up here for the last four months,” says the Weeknd. “I really haven’t been able to enjoy the fruits of my labor.” Nabil Elderkin

The world seems to agree on its perfection: _After Hours_ is one of the past year’s biggest commercial smashes, by late August raking in 1.5 million album-equivalent units in the U.S. alone, according to Alpha Data, the company that powers the _Rolling Stone_ charts. His chart-topping, Eighties-pop-inspired single “Blinding Lights” has been a fixture on the _Rolling Stone_ Top 100 Songs chart since its release, and it’s reigned for months as one of the biggest songs on TikTok, the viral-video app that has become integral to pop success over the past two years. The song even spawned its own dance challenge, involving synchronized aerobic moves meant only for the very-coordinated. (Like many other 30-year-olds, Tesfaye says he will probably never learn the “Blinding Lights” dance.)

“We work really hard, like everyone else, to maintain that mystique and maintain our original sound, and still cross over and bring it with us,” he says. “Sometimes, your fucking stars just line up.”

Still, there’s a touch of frustration in his voice as he explains why _After Hours’_ runaway success hasn’t felt quite the same as what he experienced with 2015’s _Beauty Behind the Madness_ — his first true pop blockbuster, driven by the Max Martin-produced single “Can’t Feel My Face” — or 2016’s _Starboy,_ when he teamed up with Daft Punk for an experimental pop journey. “I’ve been cooped up here for the last four months,” Tesfaye adds. “Usually you go to a club or you go driving. You hear \[your music\] on the radio. I really haven’t been able to enjoy the fruits of my labor.”

**Two years ago,** Tesfaye released a surprise EP, _My Dear Melancholy,_ that came across as a particularly dark project even by his standards, full of moody meditations that sounded like breakup songs. He headlined Coachella and began writing songs for his next full-length album. Then he decided to step on the brakes.

“I took time to live, and to live in New York,” he says. He’d always dreamed of living there, romanticizing the city his entire life. It felt even more special to give New York a try after years of being in the spotlight. On his _After Hours_ track “Escape from LA,” he says his West Coast home base “will be the end of me.” New York was Tesfaye’s excuse to take a vacation from being the Weeknd, renting a TriBeCa penthouse and living off of the celebrity grid, for the kind of paparazzi-free privacy that’s more difficult in Los Angeles.

“I got to be a normal person — go to coffee shops, write, meet new people at the bar or in the streets, make new friendships,” he says wistfully. “I felt more normal in New York than I’ll ever do anywhere else.”

Instead of continuing work on the LP he’d started writing, he detoured and wrote a secretive screenplay that he refuses to discuss in detail — just one of several such projects he’s begun dreaming up since. “I can’t talk about it too much yet,” he says. “I really want it to be official.”

Tesfaye’s love of the movies has always been a big presence in his music, videos, and tours. In the visuals for _After Hours,_ he references everything from Martin Scorsese’s dark 1985 comedy of the same name to Terry Gilliam’s 1998 adaptation of Hunter S. Thompson’s _Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas_ to Roman Polanski’s _Chinatown_ — all films that feature characters who get lost in their own lurid odysseys of sin, deceit, and excess.

In the middle of writing _After Hours,_ he got a taste of what it’s like to be on someone else’s set when the Safdie brothers recruited him for a small part in 2019’s _Uncut Gems,_ the buzzy, Oscar-robbed Adam Sandler action flick about a Diamond District jeweler with a gambling problem. Tesfaye played the 2010 version of himself: an enigmatic R&B singer on the rise whose backstage flirtation with the jeweler’s mistress prompts an onscreen fight between Tesfaye and Sandler. “After the fight, he would ask me if I was OK, and vice versa,” the singer says. “He was like an uncle. He’s a really caring guy.”

The real-life process of growing from the budding artist he plays in _Uncut Gems_ to one of the world’s biggest pop stars hasn’t left much space for Tesfaye’s big-screen dreams. “This is my first time even opening up to anything, because I had to spend the last decade invested in this project, the Weeknd,” he says. “It really does consume me, so I’ve learned to step away from it a little bit, to miss it a little bit.”

In the past year, Tesfaye has also appeared on episodes of _American Dad_ and _Robot Chicken,_ two of his favorite animated TV series. He was particularly thrilled about _American Dad,_ posting more on Instagram about his guest spot — in which he voiced an uptight, virginal cartoon version of himself — than he did about his actual album. (Admittedly, most of the posts were of the show’s resident alien, Roger, embodying each of the Weeknd’s album covers.)

“I’m an Adult Swim geek. I grew up on that,” he says. “In my dark times, they took me out of my head. \[Appearing on those shows\] was me saying, ‘Thank you for being there and making me laugh.’ Comedy’s always a big thing in my house.”

Still on his bucket list is a more universal rite of passage for musicians: a guest spot on _The Simpsons,_ another balm he’s turned to throughout his life. But when it comes to any future onscreen roles, don’t expect the Weeknd to start showing up to auditions. He still wants to be the person in control, writing or even directing projects of his own.

He may not be the first pop star to dream of breaking into Hollywood, but he’s certainly one of its most fervent fanboys. “I just want to be a filmmaker,” Tesfaye says in earnest. “I want to make great cinema.”

![Lazy loaded image](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/GRAMMY_FEA_Weekend_C.jpg?w=768)

“It might not be what people gravitate towards the most in the future. Hopefully it is. But to me, it’s definitely my most perfect album.” Nabil Elderkin

**As pandemic fears mounted** in the U.S. in the lead-up to _After Hours’_ March 20th release date, the Weeknd became one of the few major artists to stick with a previously announced album schedule for this spring. According to him, he barely even considered pushing the album back. “We had to drop it,” he says. “Imagine holding onto that record till now. It would have been a nightmare. It would have eaten me alive.”

The risk of lower streaming numbers didn’t concern him. “We went against the grain, but I didn’t care,” he says. “I didn’t even give a fuck about first week. It was all about getting that music out.”

Before quarantine began, he had begun preproduction on the recently released video for “Snowchild,” working with Japan’s first black-owned anime studio, D’ART Shtajio — prefiguring many of his peers’ recent turns to animation instead of in-person shoots. He has treatments lined up for at least three more videos (“Too Late,” “Escape from LA,” and “Faith”), though it’s unclear when he’ll be able to film them. He’s already done enough socially distant photo shoots to know that it’s not for him. “It’s weird because the connection is not there,” says Tesfaye. “It’s hard to work with a photographer when his mouth is covered. You don’t really know what he’s saying. I’d rather just wait until it goes back to normal.”

As summer wanes, he’s begun to explore other possibilities for connecting with the world, like the TikTok-hosted virtual “experience” he offered fans in lieu of his live show. His focus as the year progresses is on building out the story of _After Hours_: a lonely, dangerous, never-ending night of debauchery and chaos that could end up feeling a bit too real for everyone isolating at home.

That hasn’t left him much time to listen to new music. Asked what he’s been listening to this year, he draws a blank. He’s rooting for Roddy Ricch and Megan Thee Stallion, though, and he empathizes with the countless artists who have struggled to get their careers off the ground this year.

“A lot of new artists, they need touring,” Tesfaye says, speaking as a pop elder. “My touring is what made me the Weeknd. It was hard to show to the execs — or just to the game — that the Weeknd is more than an underground sensation. You have to bring them to the fucking shows. You have to show 15,000 people singing every single word that’s not on the radio.”

Touring was also crucial in building up his confidence early on. In his underground-sensation days, Tesfaye shrouded himself in mystery, forgoing interviews and doing his best to avoid the spotlight his music was attracting. “I tell my friends all the time it feels like my career is just starting,” he says. “I feel like it took me 10 years to break out of that shell.”

While he was doing so, his sound became a palpable influence on heroes and peers, from Drake to Beyoncé — and all the while the Weeknd moved closer to pop’s center. “I’ve always been vocal about me being a pop star,” he adds. “I thought _House of Balloons_ was pop.”

This past June, the Grammys renamed the Best Urban Contemporary Album category, in which Tesfaye has won two of his three Grammys, after Tyler, the Creator pointed out in January that it felt like a catchall for black artists making genre-bending music. “It was peculiar,” Tesfaye says of the category, which is now Progressive R&B. “Putting an album like _Starboy_ and putting an album like _Beauty Behind the Madness_ in the same category as some other artists, it’s not fair.” Both of those albums were, proudly, pop projects that ended up winning Grammys against artists as different from one another as Childish Gambino, Lianne La Havas, and SZA.

“R&B and black music is such a wide variety,” he adds. “If they put us all into one category, I still think it’s not fair. We’ll see how it goes.”

![Lazy loaded image](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/R1344-FYC-COVER-weeknd.jpg?w=844)

The Weeknd on the cover of Rolling Stone’s special Grammy preview issue. Nabil Elderkin

Tesfaye was watching closely as the protests that followed George Floyd’s killing by Minneapolis police helped prompt some much-needed music-industry reckoning. He donated $500,000 to provide legal aid and bail money for protesters as well as to the Black Lives Matter organization. He posted his receipts, and he called out his own industry to speak up for black lives after decades of profiting off of black talent — specifically naming Universal Music Group (which owns Republic), Sony, and Warner, as well as streaming services Spotify and Apple Music.

“I heard a lot of crickets,” Tesfaye says. “I just felt like, ‘You know what? I’m going to start this off. Let me just get the vibe going with this.’ I tagged everybody. I hit everybody up, too. It wasn’t just Instagram. I was like, ‘Let’s do this together for the community, for the culture. We need you guys right now.’”

The singer has kept that same energy as the year has progressed. His TikTok experience doubled as a fundraiser for the Equal Justice Initiative, a nonprofit that aims to end mass incarceration in America; viewers raised $350,000. That same week, Tesfaye donated $300,000 to Global Aid for Lebanon, following the deadly explosion in Beirut.

As for other ways the industry can better support black artists, Tesfaye has only one piece of advice he stands by. “It’s not about the upfront money,” he says. “Make sure you own your music. That’s your soul, so make sure you own it. That’s all I can really say about that.”

He was smart enough to own his masters from the start, and through his XO label, which he founded in 2010 with his creative director, La Mar Taylor, he has also been able to uplift friends like Nav, Belly, and Black Atlass. If and when he makes his long-dreamed-of movie, that will be an XO project as well.

“It will always be something that we put our 110 percent on, whatever project it is,” he says. “If it’s time for film, then everybody will be focusing on film. If it’s time for Nav, everybody’s focusing on that. If it’s time for the Weeknd, everyone’s focusing on the Weeknd. We truly believe that an empire can only be great if the heart is in it, the soul is in it.”

The Weeknd’s empire could grow by one more album by the time life returns to normal: Lately, he’s begun producing some of the new songs he’s written out of a makeshift studio in his condo.

“I might have another album ready to go by the time this quarantine is over,” he says with the slightest smirk implied in his voice, as if threatening another inescapable hit. He still finds himself feeling hungry as an artist. It’s a drive he never wants to lose, which is why he’s spent his months at home doing songwriting exercises while marathoning Korean horror films.

“I’m guilty of wanting to outdo my last album,” he says. “But it’s never like, ‘I’ve got to do the same type of song.’ I’m so happy I’m not like that. My palette is so wide.”

Accordingly, he promises, the music he’s writing is in a whole different world from _After Hours_ — a brand-new planet in the Weeknd Cinematic Universe. “I’m trying to find a perfect balance with the film and the music, and so far it’s going really well,” he says. “I think I might have cracked the code.”

_This story appears in Rolling Stone’s new stand-alone [2021 Grammys preview issue](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/2021-grammy-season-preview-1061263/), sent to music industry insiders this month._

He’s spent so much of the past decade touring the world, though, that he still sees his birthplace, Toronto, as his real home. “I didn’t realize how nice Canadians were until I left Canada,” he says.

The 30-year-old hitmaker, born Abel Tesfaye, is wearing a plain black shirt, and tomorrow he’ll reappear in a similarly understated white jersey. It’s a little jarring to see him in anything other than the slick red suit and bright-orange vintage-style frames he’s been sporting most of this year, as part of the action-packed, conceptual promotional campaign for his fourth album, _After Hours_.

As an asthmatic, Tesfaye has been taking extra precautions since the pandemic began. He works with a small group of people that includes photographer Nabil Elderkin and a few trusted affiliates and friends from his label, XO, all of whom get tested for Covid-19 every two weeks. In August, he celebrated the birthday of his Doberman, Caesar, with a cake for his “son” that he definitely didn’t bake himself. And he’s been watching movies — lots of movies, mostly ultraviolent Korean cinema. (_The Wailing,_ a 2016 horror film about a mysterious plague, and _I Saw the Devil,_ a 2010 action thriller about a man on a revenge mission, are two of his favorites.) He recently finished _Waco_ and _Unsolved Mysteries,_ among other Netflix and Hulu shows he’s been bingeing to pass the time. Sometimes he writes songs to the scenes and characters onscreen. “I’ll write about their relationship or something in a song,” he says. “It might never see the light of day. That’s an exercise. I love doing that.”

## Editor’s picks

There’s been a lot of time to fill lately, ever since he had to postpone or cancel months of touring and other promotional plans meant to follow the release of his album. “I’ve been going kind of mad, actually,” he admits.

Truthfully, though, sheltering in place hasn’t been all that different from how he usually works. Tesfaye, who has called himself a “workaholic,” put together _After Hours_ at studios in New York, Los Angeles, Toronto, and right here at home. It took two years, and he ended up building his most fully-realized world yet, an ambitious visual and musical cycle full of bruising fights, shady figures, dizzying neon lights, and inner demons. The druggy vibe and nihilistic lyrics of tracks like “Faith” and “Heartless” hearken back to a more turbulent time in his past, evoking his very public 2015 arrest for allegedly punching a Las Vegas cop, and assorted other benders.

To promote the album, he’s embraced a level of campiness he has only hinted at before, diving bloodied and bandaged nose-first into a spiraling, self-destructive character straight out of a David Lynch film. Every photo shoot, music video, and TV performance has been an extension of his fun-house-mirror world.

For Tesfaye, that immersive work scratched an itch that goes back to his earliest independent mixtapes, starting with 2011’s _House of Balloons._ The vision he brought to the photo shoots and music videos for those projects, which were compiled on 2012’s _Trilogy_ after he signed with Republic Records, created a mystique that was central to his appeal at the start of his career. “I’ve always tried to do what I do with _After Hours_ with every record I’ve ever done,” he says. “I just didn’t have the resources or the budget or the time to make them as cohesive and as singular as _After Hours_ was visually.”

The result is an album that puts him in contention for the 2021 Grammy Awards in several top categories, and one he’s immensely proud of. “It might not be my best album,” he says. “It might not be what people gravitate towards the most in the future. Hopefully it is. But to me, it’s definitely my most perfect album. I could go back and listen to it and be like, ‘I’ve got no notes for this, really.’ ”

## Related

![Lazy loaded image](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/GRAMMY_FEA_Weekend_B.jpg?w=768)

“I’ve been cooped up here for the last four months,” says the Weeknd. “I really haven’t been able to enjoy the fruits of my labor.” Nabil Elderkin

The world seems to agree on its perfection: _After Hours_ is one of the past year’s biggest commercial smashes, by late August raking in 1.5 million album-equivalent units in the U.S. alone, according to Alpha Data, the company that powers the _Rolling Stone_ charts. His chart-topping, Eighties-pop-inspired single “Blinding Lights” has been a fixture on the _Rolling Stone_ Top 100 Songs chart since its release, and it’s reigned for months as one of the biggest songs on TikTok, the viral-video app that has become integral to pop success over the past two years. The song even spawned its own dance challenge, involving synchronized aerobic moves meant only for the very-coordinated. (Like many other 30-year-olds, Tesfaye says he will probably never learn the “Blinding Lights” dance.)

“We work really hard, like everyone else, to maintain that mystique and maintain our original sound, and still cross over and bring it with us,” he says. “Sometimes, your fucking stars just line up.”

Still, there’s a touch of frustration in his voice as he explains why _After Hours’_ runaway success hasn’t felt quite the same as what he experienced with 2015’s _Beauty Behind the Madness_ — his first true pop blockbuster, driven by the Max Martin-produced single “Can’t Feel My Face” — or 2016’s _Starboy,_ when he teamed up with Daft Punk for an experimental pop journey. “I’ve been cooped up here for the last four months,” Tesfaye adds. “Usually you go to a club or you go driving. You hear \[your music\] on the radio. I really haven’t been able to enjoy the fruits of my labor.”

**Two years ago,** Tesfaye released a surprise EP, _My Dear Melancholy,_ that came across as a particularly dark project even by his standards, full of moody meditations that sounded like breakup songs. He headlined Coachella and began writing songs for his next full-length album. Then he decided to step on the brakes.

“I took time to live, and to live in New York,” he says. He’d always dreamed of living there, romanticizing the city his entire life. It felt even more special to give New York a try after years of being in the spotlight. On his _After Hours_ track “Escape from LA,” he says his West Coast home base “will be the end of me.” New York was Tesfaye’s excuse to take a vacation from being the Weeknd, renting a TriBeCa penthouse and living off of the celebrity grid, for the kind of paparazzi-free privacy that’s more difficult in Los Angeles.

“I got to be a normal person — go to coffee shops, write, meet new people at the bar or in the streets, make new friendships,” he says wistfully. “I felt more normal in New York than I’ll ever do anywhere else.”

Instead of continuing work on the LP he’d started writing, he detoured and wrote a secretive screenplay that he refuses to discuss in detail — just one of several such projects he’s begun dreaming up since. “I can’t talk about it too much yet,” he says. “I really want it to be official.”

Tesfaye’s love of the movies has always been a big presence in his music, videos, and tours. In the visuals for _After Hours,_ he references everything from Martin Scorsese’s dark 1985 comedy of the same name to Terry Gilliam’s 1998 adaptation of Hunter S. Thompson’s _Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas_ to Roman Polanski’s _Chinatown_ — all films that feature characters who get lost in their own lurid odysseys of sin, deceit, and excess.

In the middle of writing _After Hours,_ he got a taste of what it’s like to be on someone else’s set when the Safdie brothers recruited him for a small part in 2019’s _Uncut Gems,_ the buzzy, Oscar-robbed Adam Sandler action flick about a Diamond District jeweler with a gambling problem. Tesfaye played the 2010 version of himself: an enigmatic R&B singer on the rise whose backstage flirtation with the jeweler’s mistress prompts an onscreen fight between Tesfaye and Sandler. “After the fight, he would ask me if I was OK, and vice versa,” the singer says. “He was like an uncle. He’s a really caring guy.”

The real-life process of growing from the budding artist he plays in _Uncut Gems_ to one of the world’s biggest pop stars hasn’t left much space for Tesfaye’s big-screen dreams. “This is my first time even opening up to anything, because I had to spend the last decade invested in this project, the Weeknd,” he says. “It really does consume me, so I’ve learned to step away from it a little bit, to miss it a little bit.”

In the past year, Tesfaye has also appeared on episodes of _American Dad_ and _Robot Chicken,_ two of his favorite animated TV series. He was particularly thrilled about _American Dad,_ posting more on Instagram about his guest spot — in which he voiced an uptight, virginal cartoon version of himself — than he did about his actual album. (Admittedly, most of the posts were of the show’s resident alien, Roger, embodying each of the Weeknd’s album covers.)

“I’m an Adult Swim geek. I grew up on that,” he says. “In my dark times, they took me out of my head. \[Appearing on those shows\] was me saying, ‘Thank you for being there and making me laugh.’ Comedy’s always a big thing in my house.”

Still on his bucket list is a more universal rite of passage for musicians: a guest spot on _The Simpsons,_ another balm he’s turned to throughout his life. But when it comes to any future onscreen roles, don’t expect the Weeknd to start showing up to auditions. He still wants to be the person in control, writing or even directing projects of his own.

He may not be the first pop star to dream of breaking into Hollywood, but he’s certainly one of its most fervent fanboys. “I just want to be a filmmaker,” Tesfaye says in earnest. “I want to make great cinema.”

![Lazy loaded image](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/GRAMMY_FEA_Weekend_C.jpg?w=768)

“It might not be what people gravitate towards the most in the future. Hopefully it is. But to me, it’s definitely my most perfect album.” Nabil Elderkin

**As pandemic fears mounted** in the U.S. in the lead-up to _After Hours’_ March 20th release date, the Weeknd became one of the few major artists to stick with a previously announced album schedule for this spring. According to him, he barely even considered pushing the album back. “We had to drop it,” he says. “Imagine holding onto that record till now. It would have been a nightmare. It would have eaten me alive.”

The risk of lower streaming numbers didn’t concern him. “We went against the grain, but I didn’t care,” he says. “I didn’t even give a fuck about first week. It was all about getting that music out.”

Before quarantine began, he had begun preproduction on the recently released video for “Snowchild,” working with Japan’s first black-owned anime studio, D’ART Shtajio — prefiguring many of his peers’ recent turns to animation instead of in-person shoots. He has treatments lined up for at least three more videos (“Too Late,” “Escape from LA,” and “Faith”), though it’s unclear when he’ll be able to film them. He’s already done enough socially distant photo shoots to know that it’s not for him. “It’s weird because the connection is not there,” says Tesfaye. “It’s hard to work with a photographer when his mouth is covered. You don’t really know what he’s saying. I’d rather just wait until it goes back to normal.”

As summer wanes, he’s begun to explore other possibilities for connecting with the world, like the TikTok-hosted virtual “experience” he offered fans in lieu of his live show. His focus as the year progresses is on building out the story of _After Hours_: a lonely, dangerous, never-ending night of debauchery and chaos that could end up feeling a bit too real for everyone isolating at home.

That hasn’t left him much time to listen to new music. Asked what he’s been listening to this year, he draws a blank. He’s rooting for Roddy Ricch and Megan Thee Stallion, though, and he empathizes with the countless artists who have struggled to get their careers off the ground this year.

“A lot of new artists, they need touring,” Tesfaye says, speaking as a pop elder. “My touring is what made me the Weeknd. It was hard to show to the execs — or just to the game — that the Weeknd is more than an underground sensation. You have to bring them to the fucking shows. You have to show 15,000 people singing every single word that’s not on the radio.”

Touring was also crucial in building up his confidence early on. In his underground-sensation days, Tesfaye shrouded himself in mystery, forgoing interviews and doing his best to avoid the spotlight his music was attracting. “I tell my friends all the time it feels like my career is just starting,” he says. “I feel like it took me 10 years to break out of that shell.”

While he was doing so, his sound became a palpable influence on heroes and peers, from Drake to Beyoncé — and all the while the Weeknd moved closer to pop’s center. “I’ve always been vocal about me being a pop star,” he adds. “I thought _House of Balloons_ was pop.”

This past June, the Grammys renamed the Best Urban Contemporary Album category, in which Tesfaye has won two of his three Grammys, after Tyler, the Creator pointed out in January that it felt like a catchall for black artists making genre-bending music. “It was peculiar,” Tesfaye says of the category, which is now Progressive R&B. “Putting an album like _Starboy_ and putting an album like _Beauty Behind the Madness_ in the same category as some other artists, it’s not fair.” Both of those albums were, proudly, pop projects that ended up winning Grammys against artists as different from one another as Childish Gambino, Lianne La Havas, and SZA.

“R&B and black music is such a wide variety,” he adds. “If they put us all into one category, I still think it’s not fair. We’ll see how it goes.”

![Lazy loaded image](https://www.rollingstone.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/09/R1344-FYC-COVER-weeknd.jpg?w=844)

The Weeknd on the cover of Rolling Stone’s special Grammy preview issue. Nabil Elderkin

Tesfaye was watching closely as the protests that followed George Floyd’s killing by Minneapolis police helped prompt some much-needed music-industry reckoning. He donated $500,000 to provide legal aid and bail money for protesters as well as to the Black Lives Matter organization. He posted his receipts, and he called out his own industry to speak up for black lives after decades of profiting off of black talent — specifically naming Universal Music Group (which owns Republic), Sony, and Warner, as well as streaming services Spotify and Apple Music.

“I heard a lot of crickets,” Tesfaye says. “I just felt like, ‘You know what? I’m going to start this off. Let me just get the vibe going with this.’ I tagged everybody. I hit everybody up, too. It wasn’t just Instagram. I was like, ‘Let’s do this together for the community, for the culture. We need you guys right now.’”

The singer has kept that same energy as the year has progressed. His TikTok experience doubled as a fundraiser for the Equal Justice Initiative, a nonprofit that aims to end mass incarceration in America; viewers raised $350,000. That same week, Tesfaye donated $300,000 to Global Aid for Lebanon, following the deadly explosion in Beirut.

As for other ways the industry can better support black artists, Tesfaye has only one piece of advice he stands by. “It’s not about the upfront money,” he says. “Make sure you own your music. That’s your soul, so make sure you own it. That’s all I can really say about that.”

He was smart enough to own his masters from the start, and through his XO label, which he founded in 2010 with his creative director, La Mar Taylor, he has also been able to uplift friends like Nav, Belly, and Black Atlass. If and when he makes his long-dreamed-of movie, that will be an XO project as well.

“It will always be something that we put our 110 percent on, whatever project it is,” he says. “If it’s time for film, then everybody will be focusing on film. If it’s time for Nav, everybody’s focusing on that. If it’s time for the Weeknd, everyone’s focusing on the Weeknd. We truly believe that an empire can only be great if the heart is in it, the soul is in it.”

The Weeknd’s empire could grow by one more album by the time life returns to normal: Lately, he’s begun producing some of the new songs he’s written out of a makeshift studio in his condo.

“I might have another album ready to go by the time this quarantine is over,” he says with the slightest smirk implied in his voice, as if threatening another inescapable hit. He still finds himself feeling hungry as an artist. It’s a drive he never wants to lose, which is why he’s spent his months at home doing songwriting exercises while marathoning Korean horror films.

“I’m guilty of wanting to outdo my last album,” he says. “But it’s never like, ‘I’ve got to do the same type of song.’ I’m so happy I’m not like that. My palette is so wide.”

Accordingly, he promises, the music he’s writing is in a whole different world from _After Hours_ — a brand-new planet in the Weeknd Cinematic Universe. “I’m trying to find a perfect balance with the film and the music, and so far it’s going really well,” he says. “I think I might have cracked the code.”

_This story appears in Rolling Stone’s new stand-alone [2021 Grammys preview issue](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/2021-grammy-season-preview-1061263/), sent to music industry insiders this month._

_**Dawn FM**_ is the fifth studio album by Canadian singer-songwriter [the Weeknd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weeknd "The Weeknd"). It was released on January 7, 2022, by [XO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XO_\(record_label\) "XO (record label)") and [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). The album contains [guest appearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guest_appearance "Guest appearance") by [Tyler, the Creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_the_Creator "Tyler, the Creator") and [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne") and narration by [Jim Carrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Carrey "Jim Carrey"), [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones"), and [Josh Safdie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safdie_brothers "Safdie brothers"). Production was primarily handled by the Weeknd alongside a variety of producers, including [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), [OPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneohtrix_Point_Never "Oneohtrix Point Never"), [Oscar Holter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Holter "Oscar Holter"), [Swedish House Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_House_Mafia "Swedish House Mafia"), and [Calvin Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Harris "Calvin Harris"), among others.

_Dawn FM_ is a generally upbeat record containing [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop "Dance-pop") and [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") songs heavily inspired by 1980s [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [electronic dance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music"). Conceptually, the Weeknd described the album as reflecting [purgatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purgatory "Purgatory"), while critics noted it explores psychedelic and [existential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism") themes. It is also the second instalment in a trilogy of albums, following _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ (2020) and preceding _[Hurry Up Tomorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurry_Up_Tomorrow "Hurry Up Tomorrow")_ (2025).

_**Dawn FM**_ is the fifth studio album by Canadian singer-songwriter [the Weeknd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weeknd "The Weeknd"). It was released on January 7, 2022, by [XO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XO_\(record_label\) "XO (record label)") and [Republic Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_Records "Republic Records"). The album contains [guest appearances](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guest_appearance "Guest appearance") by [Tyler, the Creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_the_Creator "Tyler, the Creator") and [Lil Wayne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_Wayne "Lil Wayne") and narration by [Jim Carrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Carrey "Jim Carrey"), [Quincy Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quincy_Jones "Quincy Jones"), and [Josh Safdie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safdie_brothers "Safdie brothers"). Production was primarily handled by the Weeknd alongside a variety of producers, including [Max Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Martin "Max Martin"), [OPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneohtrix_Point_Never "Oneohtrix Point Never"), [Oscar Holter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oscar_Holter "Oscar Holter"), [Swedish House Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_House_Mafia "Swedish House Mafia"), and [Calvin Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Harris "Calvin Harris"), among others.

_Dawn FM_ is a generally upbeat record containing [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop "Dance-pop") and [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop") songs heavily inspired by 1980s [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"), [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"), and [electronic dance music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music"). Conceptually, the Weeknd described the album as reflecting [purgatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purgatory "Purgatory"), while critics noted it explores psychedelic and [existential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existentialism "Existentialism") themes. It is also the second instalment in a trilogy of albums, following _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ (2020) and preceding _[Hurry Up Tomorrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurry_Up_Tomorrow "Hurry Up Tomorrow")_ (2025).

_Dawn FM_ was supported by four singles—"[Take My Breath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_My_Breath "Take My Breath")", "[Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrifice_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Sacrifice (The Weeknd song)")", "[Out of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_Time_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Out of Time (The Weeknd song)")" and "[Less than Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Less_than_Zero_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Less than Zero (The Weeknd song)")"—with "Take My Breath" peaking at number six on the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100"). The album opened with first-week sales of 148,000 [album-equivalent units](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album-equivalent_unit "Album-equivalent unit") in the U.S. and debuted at number two on the [_Billboard_ 200](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_200 "Billboard 200"). Internationally, it peaked at number one in 11 countries, including Australia, Canada, the Netherlands, Ireland, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom. _Dawn FM_ received widespread acclaim from critics, with praise for its production, song structures, and melodies.

## Background and release

On March 20, 2020, [the Weeknd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Weeknd "The Weeknd") released his fourth studio album _[After Hours](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/After_Hours_\(The_Weeknd_album\) "After Hours (The Weeknd album)")_ during the beginning of [COVID-19 restrictions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_lockdowns "COVID-19 lockdowns").[\[1\]](#cite_note-1) It was a commercial success and received mostly positive reviews from [music critics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Music_journalism "Music journalism"), some of whom named it his best work yet.[\[2\]](#cite_note-2)[\[3\]](#cite_note-3) Shortly after, the Weeknd began working on his next studio album; in an interview with _[Rolling Stone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rolling_Stone "Rolling Stone")_ in September 2020, he stated that he "might have another album ready to go by the time this quarantine is over."[\[4\]](#cite_note-4) The Weeknd later explained that he was originally working on an album inspired by the [depressive state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depression_\(mood\) "Depression (mood)") he was in during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"), but scrapped the project because it was "emotionally detrimental" and began working on _Dawn FM_.[\[5\]](#cite_note-5)

The Weeknd began to tease a new album in May 2021 in an interview with _[Variety](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Variety_\(magazine\) "Variety (magazine)")_, when he stated "if the last record is the _After Hours_ of the night, then _The Dawn_ is coming".[\[6\]](#cite_note-6) He continued to tease the album with the [tentative title](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Working_title "Working title"), _The Dawn_, during his acceptance speeches at the [2021 _Billboard_ Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Billboard_Music_Awards "2021 Billboard Music Awards") and the [2021 iHeartRadio Music Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_iHeartRadio_Music_Awards "2021 iHeartRadio Music Awards").[\[7\]](#cite_note-7) On August 2, the Weeknd released a teaser on his social media accounts titled "The Dawn Is Coming", which contained a snippet of a then-unreleased song. Later that day, in a partnership with [NBC Sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC_Sports "NBC Sports") and the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics"), he announced the album's lead single "[Take My Breath](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_My_Breath "Take My Breath")", which was released on August 6.[\[8\]](#cite_note-release-8) On October 4, 2021, during an episode of his [Apple Music 1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Music_1 "Apple Music 1") radio show, _[Memento Mori](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memento_Mori_\(radio_show\) "Memento Mori (radio show)")_, the Weeknd announced that the album was complete, and that he was waiting on a "couple characters that are key to the narrative." He then described the characters as "some people that are near and dear to me, some people that inspired my life as a child and some that inspire me now."[\[9\]](#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](#cite_note-10)

# Dawn FM

2, the Weeknd teased a possible [surprise release of the album](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surprise_album "Surprise album") in an [Instagram](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Instagram "Instagram") post, which featured a screenshot of a text conversation he had with his best friend and creative director [La Mar Taylor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Mar_Taylor "La Mar Taylor"). After exchanging [New Year's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Year's_Day "New Year's Day") greetings, the Weeknd messaged that "Everything feels chaotic again. Music can heal and that feels more important than another album rollout. Let's just drop the whole thing and enjoy it with the people... XO."[\[11\]](#cite_note-11) The next day, the Weeknd hinted at the album's arrival, tweeting "wake up at dawn tomorrow".[\[12\]](#cite_note-12) On January 3, he announced the album's official title through a trailer video and announced that it would be released on January 7, 2022.[\[13\]](#cite_note-13) He subsequently revealed the track listing through a second trailer on January 5.[\[14\]](#cite_note-Track_listing-14) On January 11, the Weeknd announced an expanded edition of the album subtitled _Alternate World_ including two remixes and previously released single "[Moth to a Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moth_to_a_Flame "Moth to a Flame")" with [Swedish House Mafia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swedish_House_Mafia "Swedish House Mafia").[\[15\]](#cite_note-Kaufman2-15)

## Composition

> Who knows what the next one is going to sound like? When it comes to my albums, there is a cohesive sound going on, but I can't really stick to one style. So you'll hear [EDM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_dance_music "Electronic dance music"), [hip-hop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hip_hop_music "Hip hop music") and three other types of sounds in one song – and somehow, we make it work.

_Dawn FM_ has been primarily described as [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pop_music "Pop music"),[\[17\]](#cite_note-Stereogum-17) [synth-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synth-pop "Synth-pop"),[\[18\]](#cite_note-Paste-18) [dance-pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance-pop "Dance-pop"),[\[17\]](#cite_note-Stereogum-17) and [R&B](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_R&B "Contemporary R&B").[\[19\]](#cite_note-19) Recalling [1980s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980s_in_music "1980s in music") [electronic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electronic_music "Electronic music") bands such as [Depeche Mode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Depeche_Mode "Depeche Mode") and [Duran Duran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duran_Duran "Duran Duran"),[\[20\]](#cite_note-O'Connor-20)[\[21\]](#cite_note-TLofBF-21)[\[22\]](#cite_note-NME-22) the album significantly incorporates [new wave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_wave_music "New wave music"),[\[23\]](#cite_note-Exclaim!_Rev-23) [funk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funk "Funk"),[\[24\]](#cite_note-MTV-24) and EDM,[\[16\]](#cite_note-Mamo-16) alongside elements of [disco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disco "Disco"),[\[25\]](#cite_note-Moreland-25) [electropop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electropop "Electropop"),[\[23\]](#cite_note-Exclaim!_Rev-23) hip hop,[\[23\]](#cite_note-Exclaim!_Rev-23)[\[16\]](#cite_note-Mamo-16) [city pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_pop "City pop"),[\[21\]](#cite_note-TLofBF-21) [soft rock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_rock "Soft rock"),[\[26\]](#cite_note-26) [psychedelia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_music "Psychedelic music"),[\[27\]](#cite_note-Olivier-27) [blues](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blues "Blues"),[\[28\]](#cite_note-Consequence-28) [boogie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boogie_\(genre\) "Boogie (genre)"), [electro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electro_\(music\) "Electro (music)"),[\[17\]](#cite_note-Stereogum-17) and [techno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Techno "Techno").[\[18\]](#cite_note-Paste-18)

During an episode of _Memento Mori_, the Weeknd cited [Britney Spears](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Britney_Spears "Britney Spears"), [Nas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nas "Nas"), Swedish House Mafia, [Kid Cudi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_Cudi "Kid Cudi"), [Kanye West](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanye_West "Kanye West") and [Tyler, the Creator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyler,_the_Creator "Tyler, the Creator") as the artists who have inspired the album.[\[29\]](#cite_note-29) Influences of [Michael Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Jackson "Michael Jackson")'s _[Off the Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Off_the_Wall "Off the Wall")_ (1979) and _[Thriller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thriller_\(album\) "Thriller (album)")_ (1982) are also present in _Dawn FM_.[\[28\]](#cite_note-Consequence-28)

### Concept and themes

_Dawn FM_ was noted for incorporating a "[psychedelic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Psychedelic_art "Psychedelic art") radio" aesthetic with [existential](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Existential_crisis "Existential crisis") themes,[\[30\]](#cite_note-30) similar to American [experimental](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experimental_music "Experimental music") record producer [Oneohtrix Point Never](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oneohtrix_Point_Never "Oneohtrix Point Never")'s album _[Magic Oneohtrix Point Never](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_Oneohtrix_Point_Never "Magic Oneohtrix Point Never")_ (2020), which the Weeknd appeared on and executive produced under his formal name.[\[31\]](#cite_note-31) The "103.5" station tag that the album frequently uses is a nod to the Toronto radio station [Z103.5](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIDC-FM "CIDC-FM"), known for their [dance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dance_music "Dance music")\-heavy playlists.[\[32\]](#cite_note-32) In an interview with _Billboard_ on November 23, 2021, the Weeknd elaborated on these themes, saying:

> Picture the album being like the listener is dead. And they're stuck in this [purgatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purgatory "Purgatory") state, which I always imagined would be like being stuck in traffic waiting to reach the light at the end of the tunnel. And while you're stuck in traffic, they got a radio station playing in the car, with a radio host guiding you to the light and helping you transition to the other side. So it could feel celebratory, could feel bleak, however you want to make it feel, but that's what _The Dawn_ is for me.[\[16\]](#cite_note-Mamo-16)

Further speculation on the album's concept arose following the Weeknd's announcement that _Dawn FM_ was the second part of a [trilogy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trilogy "Trilogy") of albums.[\[33\]](#cite_note-33)

## Artwork

The standard and _Alternate World_ editions' [album cover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Album_cover "Album cover") of _Dawn FM_ was shot by Matilda Finn.[\[34\]](#cite_note-Kaufman-34) It features a "dramatically aged version" of the Weeknd as an elderly and overweight bearded man in a dark background setting with a small ray of light shining behind the back of his shoulder.[\[35\]](#cite_note-35) The [collector's and limited editions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_edition "Special edition") of the album, as well as the limited edition boxset CDs of the album, listed on the Weeknd's online store, feature five alternate _Dawn FM_ covers designed by American artist [Robert Beatty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Beatty_\(artist\) "Robert Beatty (artist)").[\[36\]](#cite_note-36)

### Singles

On August 6, 2021, the album's lead single, "Take My Breath", was released digitally on music stores and streaming services.[\[8\]](#cite_note-release-8) The song peaked at number six on the US [_Billboard_ Hot 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Billboard_Hot_100 "Billboard Hot 100") and reached the top ten in 21 other territories.[\[37\]](#cite_note-37) Its music video was premiered alongside its release and was directed by Cliqua.[\[38\]](#cite_note-38) An official remix by Italian [house music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_music "House music") group Agents of Time was released with the original version of the _Alternate World_ edition of the album on January 11, 2022.[\[39\]](#cite_note-39)

"[Sacrifice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacrifice_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Sacrifice (The Weeknd song)")" was released as the second official single in tandem with _Dawn FM_ on January 7, 2022.[\[40\]](#cite_note-40) Its music video was released on the same day, and was directed by Cliqua.[\[41\]](#cite_note-41) The song was sent to [contemporary hit radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contemporary_hit_radio "Contemporary hit radio") in the United States on January 11, 2022.[\[42\]](#cite_note-42)

"[Out of Time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out_of_Time_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Out of Time (The Weeknd song)")" was released to American [urban adult contemporary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Urban_adult_contemporary "Urban adult contemporary") radio on January 25, 2022, as the third official single from the album.[\[43\]](#cite_note-43) Its music video was released on April 5, 2022, and was directed by Cliqua.[\[44\]](#cite_note-44) An official remix of the song by Haitian-Canadian music producer [Kaytranada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaytranada "Kaytranada") was released on April 22, 2022, and later included on the streaming reissue of the _Alternate World_ edition of the album.[\[45\]](#cite_note-45)

"[Less than Zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Less_than_Zero_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Less than Zero (The Weeknd song)")" was given a limited single release in France, with it being sent to contemporary hit radio on July 7, 2022, as the album's fourth single in the country.[\[46\]](#cite_note-46)

### Promotional singles

On July 1, 2022, an official remix of the album's eleventh track "Starry Eyes" by [Mike Dean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dean_\(music_producer\) "Mike Dean (music producer)") was released as the f

On July 22, 2022, a remix of the album's third track "[How Do I Make You Love Me?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_Do_I_Make_You_Love_Me%3F "How Do I Make You Love Me?")" by Swedish House Mafia members [Sebastian Ingrosso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastian_Ingrosso "Sebastian Ingrosso") and [Salvatore Ganacci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvatore_Ganacci "Salvatore Ganacci") was released as the third promotional single from the streaming re-issue of the _Alternate World_ edition of the album.[\[52\]](#cite_note-52)[\[53\]](#cite_note-53)[\[54\]](#cite_note-54) Simultaneously, an animated music video for the original version of the song was released that same day. It was directed by Jocelyn Charles with some creative direction from Cliqua.[\[55\]](#cite_note-55)

An official remix of the album's ninth track "Best Friends" with American R&B singer [Summer Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Walker "Summer Walker") was released as the fourth and final promotional single of the streaming re-issue of the _Alternate World_ edition of the album on August 5, 2022.[\[56\]](#cite_note-56)[\[57\]](#cite_note-57)[\[58\]](#cite_note-58)

### Other songs

A music video for the album's second track "[Gasoline](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gasoline_\(The_Weeknd_song\) "Gasoline (The Weeknd song)")" was released on January 11, 2022.[\[59\]](#cite_note-59) It was directed by Matilda Finn.[\[34\]](#cite_note-Kaufman-34) On January 7, 2023, a music video for the album's tenth track "[Is There Someone Else?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is_There_Someone_Else%3F "Is There Someone Else?")" was released, as part of the one-year anniversary of the album's release. It was directed by Cliqua.[\[60\]](#cite_note-60)[\[61\]](#cite_note-61)

### _103.5 Dawn FM_ livestream

On January 7, 2022, alongside the release of _Dawn FM_, the Weeknd hosted a live event with [Amazon Music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Music "Amazon Music"), in which he served as a [disc jockey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Disc_jockey "Disc jockey") and played the entire album in front of a small crowd.[\[62\]](#cite_note-62) The event was live-streamed on [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_\(service\) "Twitch (service)") and was directed by Micah Bickham.[\[63\]](#cite_note-63) Various different shots of the livestream were turned into lyric videos for the album.[\[64\]](#cite_note-64) The whole livestream was uploaded to [YouTube](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/YouTube "YouTube") on January 12, 2022.

### _The Dawn FM Experience_

On February 21, 2022, the Weeknd announced _The Dawn FM Experience_, a television music special with [Amazon Prime Video](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amazon_Prime_Video "Amazon Prime Video") that premiered on February 26. The special was directed by Micah Bickham and features live performances, theater and performance art for a "night out at the club."[\[65\]](#cite_note-65) A ten-track live [EP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extended_play "Extended play") composed of the songs the Weeknd performed during the special was made available to stream exclusively on Amazon Music.[\[66\]](#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](#cite_note-67) _The Dawn FM Experience_ entered the [UK Albums Chart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Albums_Chart "UK Albums Chart") in March 2022, peaking at number 92.[\[68\]](#cite_note-68)

### Tour

Originally set to only support _After Hours_, the Weeknd announced on October 18, 2021, that his upcoming seventh [concert tour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concert_tour "Concert tour") would be renamed as the After Hours til Dawn Tour to incorporate elements from _Dawn FM_.[\[69\]](#cite_note-69)
